title: Depend on a small interface
summary: Replace a concrete notifier with a consumer-defined interface and propagate errors.

scenario.briefing: SendAll accepts only *EmailNotifier, so tests cannot substitute a fake and notification errors disappear. Define the behavior SendAll needs and propagate failures.

objectives.description: Define and accept a small notifier interface.
Choose where a Go interface belongs.
Explain implicit satisfaction and error propagation accurately.

hints: Declare an interface with that one method.
Accept the interface in the function signature.
Return the error from Notify instead of ignoring it.

misconceptions.description: Accepting a concrete notifier instead of the behavior.
misconceptions.testDescription: SendAll accepts the interface, not a concrete notifier.
misconceptions.feedback: A concrete parameter forces every caller to use that type. Accept the small interface SendAll actually needs.

misconceptions.description: Declaring the interface in the implementing package by habit.
misconceptions.feedback: Go interfaces are usually declared by the consumer. That keeps the contract small and avoids import cycles.

misconceptions.description: Believing an interface holding a typed nil is itself nil.
misconceptions.feedback: An interface value is nil only when both its type and value are nil. A typed nil pointer inside an interface is not nil.

sections.title: Interfaces are satisfied implicitly
sections.body: A Go type implements an interface by defining its methods. There is no implements clause. This keeps the contract at the consumer: a package can declare the small interface it needs and accept any type that already provides those methods.

sections.title: Small interfaces travel well
sections.body: The standard library's io.Reader and io.Writer are small for a reason. A one- or two-method interface is easy to implement and easy to fake in a test. Large interfaces couple the caller to details it does not use.

sections.title: Return errors, do not hide them
sections.body: A method that can fail returns an error. The caller checks it and decides whether to stop, retry, or wrap it. An interface method that returns error gives every implementation a uniform way to report failure.

vocabulary.definition: A set of method signatures that a type satisfies implicitly.
An interface declared by the package that uses it, not the package that implements it.
Go's built-in interface for representing failure.
An interface value with no dynamic type or value.

steps.title: Interfaces and errors

statements.label: A type satisfies an interface by implementing its methods, without an explicit declaration.
Small interfaces are easier to implement and fake in tests.
An interface holding a typed nil pointer is itself nil.
An interface method can return error so callers can handle failure.

steps.explanation: Go interfaces are implicit and benefit from being small. A typed nil inside an interface still carries a type, and errors are ordinary return values.
hints: A nil pointer stored in an interface has a dynamic type.
